problem: Saying "React does not use HTML's onchange attribute" overstates it. React does have an onChange prop, but it is camelCase and fires on every keystroke, while the HTML onchange attribute fires when the field loses focus or its value is committed. A student can read the sentence as "React has no change event at all".
fix: React uses camelCase event props such as onChange, not the HTML onchange attribute, and its onChange fires on every keystroke instead of only when the field loses focus.

problem: The claim that React Hook Form or Formik are used "to avoid one state update per keystroke" is wrong for Formik. Formik stores field values in its own state and re-renders on each keystroke; only React Hook Form, which reads inputs through refs (uncontrolled by default), avoids the per-keystroke state update.
fix: Libraries such as React Hook Form keep inputs uncontrolled and read them through refs, so they skip a state update per keystroke; Formik is built on controlled inputs and still updates on each keystroke.

problem: Both messages "onChange fires" and "setName('R')" are drawn from Input to React state, so the diagram shows the input writing state, which contradicts Section 3's point that only the handler calls the setter.
fix: Keep "onChange fires" from Input to React state and label the second message "handler calls setName('R')", or add the handler as the middle participant between Input and React state.
